readerTitle: Same crate, two factories: why one stopped fighting for shelf space
caseNote: 가상 사례 (단열 크레이트를 만드는 두 공장, 러닝화 매장) · Ries & Trout의 '카테고리의 법칙'을 원리로 인용
insight: 기존 카테고리에서 더 나은 제품이 되려 하기보다, 내가 처음인 새 카테고리를 정의하면 고객의 비교 기준 자체가 바뀐다.
misconception: 제품이 더 좋으면 기존 시장의 1등 브랜드와 같은 진열대에서도 이길 수 있다. 새 카테고리는 이름만 새로 붙이면 된다.

sources.text: Ries, A. & Trout, J. (1993). The 22 Immutable Laws of Marketing. HarperBusiness. (The Law of the Category)

factChecks.note: 4번 카드는 Ries & Trout의 '카테고리의 법칙'(If you can't be first in a category, set up a new category you can be first in)을 직접 인용하지 않고 의역했습니다. 원문 문구와 출간 연도(1993)를 게시 전에 확인하세요.
두 공장, 빵집, 이삿짐 회사, 러닝화 매장은 모두 가상 사례입니다. 결과(가격 결정권, 기준 사양서 작성 등)는 설명용 서사이며 실제 데이터가 아닙니다.

cards.title: Same crate, two answers to "What is it?"
body: Two small factories make almost the same thing: a light, insulated plastic crate that keeps food cold for hours.
One sells it as a cooler. The other sells it as something nobody has bought before. Only one of them gets to set the terms.

image.label: Two identical crates with different labels
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 똑같이 생긴 단열 크레이트 두 개가 나란히 놓여 있음. 왼쪽 라벨 "Cooler", 오른쪽 라벨 "Delivery cold crate". 왼쪽 뒤로는 비슷한 쿨러들이 빽빽한 진열대, 오른쪽 뒤로는 텅 빈 공간. 실제 브랜드 로고 없음.

cards.title: How do you describe your crate?
body: You make the crate. It's lighter than most coolers and keeps food cold about two hours longer.
Famous outdoor brands own the cooler aisle, with budgets you can't match. What do you tell buyers it is?

options.text: A better cooler: lighter, and cold for longer
options.feedback: True and clear. But it puts you in a line-up with famous brands, where buyers judge you on their terms and your budget is the smallest.

options.text: The best-value cooler on the market
options.feedback: Price is easy to understand and easy to copy. A bigger rival can afford to cut prices for longer than you can.

options.text: A returnable cold crate for grocery and meal delivery firms
options.feedback: You give up the big consumer aisle. In return, buyers have nothing to compare you with, so you become the standard.

cards.title: One fought for shelf space. One wrote the rules.
body: Factory A's crate landed on shelves next to the big brands. Stores wanted a discount to stock an unknown name. Every sales talk started with "Why not the famous one?"
Factory B pitched delivery firms that were losing food in warm vans. There was no leading cold crate to compare against. B's spec sheet became the list buyers used to judge everyone who came later.

image.label: Factory A in a crowded aisle, Factory B alone
image.brief: 화면을 반으로 나눈 일러스트. 왼쪽: 쿨러가 가득한 매장 진열대 구석에 작게 놓인 A 크레이트와 할인 스티커. 오른쪽: 배달 밴 옆에서 B 크레이트를 열어보는 배달 회사 직원, 주변에 비교 대상 없음. 실제 로고 없음.

cards.title: Creating a category
body: **Creating a category** means defining a new kind of product or service, so customers stop comparing you with the leaders of an old one.
In the new category, you're first by default. And the first name in a category often becomes the one others are measured against.
Marketers Al Ries and Jack Trout made this a rule in their 1993 book *The 22 Immutable Laws of Marketing*: if you can't be first in a category, set up a new one you can be first in.

cards.title: Why a new box beats a better product.
body: Customers sort what they buy into mental boxes. They pick the box first, then the brand inside it.
list: **Old box:** "cooler". The leader is already chosen. You must prove you beat it.
**New box:** "cold crate for delivery". No leader yet. You can be the answer.
**The question changes:** from "Which one is best?" to "Do I need this?"
cards.callout: That last question takes more work to answer. But once the answer is yes, you're the default.
cards.softwareNote: Software founders often do this by naming a new type of tool instead of claiming to be a better version of an existing one. The name only sticks if the product really works differently from what buyers already use.

cards.title: It works in any industry.
body: A bakery stops selling "pastries" and starts selling "breakfast boxes for office meetings". A moving company becomes "office moves done over one weekend".
In each case, the business picks buyers with a specific problem the old category serves badly. Then it names the new thing after that problem, not after the product.

image.label: A bakery box and a moving truck with new labels
image.brief: 플랫 일러스트. 왼쪽: 회의실 테이블 위 "Breakfast box for meetings" 라벨이 붙은 빵 상자. 오른쪽: 금요일 밤에 출발해 월요일 아침 정리된 사무실로 이어지는 이삿짐 트럭. 실제 상호나 로고 없음.

cards.title: A new category has to be sold twice.
body: First you sell the idea that the category should exist. Then you sell your product. That takes time and money, and some new categories never find enough buyers.
A new name on an old product doesn't count. Customers see through it. And if the category works, rivals will follow, so you still have to earn the lead.

cards.title: Now it's a running shoe shop.
body: A big sports chain opens down the road with more brands and lower prices.
Many of your loyal customers are runners with sore knees or feet who come in for advice. What do you become?

options.text: The best running shoe store in town
options.feedback: It keeps your current customers comfortable. But it invites a direct comparison with a chain that wins on range and price.

options.text: A fitting clinic for runners with sore feet, with trained fitters and gait checks
options.feedback: You serve fewer people, but the chain isn't really in this category. You'd need to keep investing in the skills that make it real.

options.text: Rename the shop "Run Lab" and keep everything else the same
options.feedback: A fresh name costs little. But with nothing new behind it, customers will still compare you with the chain, and lose interest fast.

cards.title: If you can't win the race, start a new one.
body: Don't only ask how to beat the leader. Ask what new kind of thing you could be first at, for buyers the old category serves badly.
**Try it today:** finish the sentence "We're the only ___ for ___." If you can't fill it with something true, you're still competing in someone else's category.
